title: Chapter 6: Model-View-Controller (MVC) Pattern
summary: Model–View–Controller (MVC) is a design pattern in Human–Computer Interaction and software design that divides a system into three distinct parts—Model, View, and Controller—to make programs easier to build, understand, and maintain.

sections.title: Introduction to Model–View–Controller (MVC)
paragraphs: Model–View–Controller (MVC) is a design pattern in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) and software design.
Purpose: To make programs easier to build, understand, and fix.
Think of MVC like a restaurant:
list: Model – the brain (data & logic) / kitchen (where the food is prepared = data/logic)
View – the face (what you see) / menu + food served (what the customer sees)
Controller – the hands (what you do) / waiter (takes your order and delivers it between kitchen and you)

sections.title: Model (The Brain of the System)
paragraphs: Stores and manages the system’s data and rules.
Without the Model, the program has no knowledge to show.
list: Knows everything about the system’s content.
Updates data when something changes.
Does not care about how things look on screen.

sections.title: View (The Face of the System)
paragraphs: The visual representation of the data.
Without the View, users can’t see or interact with the data.
list: Shows information to the user in a friendly way.
Changes automatically when the Model updates.

sections.title: Controller (The Hands of the System)
paragraphs: Acts as a bridge between the user and the system.
Without the Controller, the user cannot communicate with the system.
list: Takes input from the user (clicks, taps, voice, typing).
Decides what action to perform.
Tells the Model or View what to do.

sections.title: How MVC Works Together (Flow)
list: User does something (click, tap, type) -> handled by Controller.
Controller updates the Model (changes data).
Model notifies the View of changes.
View shows the updated information to the User.

sections.title: Benefits of MVC
list: Separation of roles: Each part has its own job.
Easy to maintain: Designers can work on View, programmers on Model.
Reusability: One Model can work with different Views.
Flexibility: Changes in one part don’t break the others.

sections.title: Quick Analogy Recap
paragraphs: Remember: MVC is like teamwork. Each part has its own responsibility, and together they make the system run smoothly.
list: Restaurant: Kitchen (Model), Waiter (Controller), Served food (View).
Human body: Brain (Model), Hands (Controller), Face (View).
Music app: Song data (Model), Playlist screen (View), Play button (Controller).

title: Chapter 5: Usability and User Experience Evaluation
summary: Evaluating a user interface ensures that the system is easy to use (usability), the experience is positive and enjoyable (UX), and the process is safe, ethical, and user-centered.

sections.title: Usability
paragraphs: Usability is about how easy, efficient, and effective a system is to use.
list: Quantitative: Measured through performance tasks (e.g., how many clicks, how much time it takes to complete an action).
Qualitative: Based on user opinions, feedback, and surveys (e.g., how simple or tiring the system feels).
Usability Survey: Often includes questions involving the ease of use, ease of learning, fatigue, simple preference, and other questions specific to the given interface.

sections.title: User Experience (UX)
paragraphs: UX is more than usability it’s about the overall feeling, satisfaction, and emotional connection users have while interacting with the system. Covers how enjoyable, intuitive, and stress-free the app feels.

sections.title: Interview / Observation
paragraphs: The simplest way: talk to users or watch them use the system. Helps identify problems that designers might miss.

sections.title: Cognitive Walkthrough
paragraphs: Users “think aloud” while using the system. They describe what they are doing and why. This reveals their thought process and points of confusion.

sections.title: Expert Heuristic Evaluation
paragraphs: Usability experts review the system using established principles called heuristics.
list: Visibility of system status
Match between system and the real world
User control and freedom
Consistency and standards
Error prevention
Recognition rather than recall
Flexibility and efficiency of use
Aesthetic and minimalist design
Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
Help and documentation

sections.title: Measurement
paragraphs: Collect numerical or survey-based data to measure effectiveness. Can involve time, error rates, or satisfaction scores.

sections.title: Safety & Ethics
paragraphs: Evaluations must be safe and respectful. Users should give informed consent before participating. Participants should always have the right to stop whenever they feel uncomfortable.

sections.title: Summary
paragraphs: Evaluating a user interface ensures that:
list: The system is easy to use (usability)
The experience is positive and enjoyable (UX)
The process is safe, ethical, and user-centered
